event: On Day 5 Wren wakes to the basin thrush calling in fours: check the sky.
A soft grey cloud ceiling has moved in; the air smells mineral, of the plateau.
It is the high wind the Shelf relayed on Day 3, two days reaching the basin floor.
Theron is at the rebuilt fire; they drink tea without speaking.
He looks north-east, toward the ruins: 'The east structure. Hadley's slab.'
A ghost elm grew its lateral roots to catch the slab when it fell, forty or fifty years ago.
'We should see it properly.' 'Yes. After Maret.'
Hadley comes out for flatcakes with a full theory of root geometry in the ruins.
Maret will arrive by midday; Hadley agrees not to narrate his root theory at her.
In cloud-light the ruins flatten and look older; the shimmer is softer.
At the east structure a fallen roof slab shelters a space two people long.
Three ghost-elm roots brace it from below, root and stone worn to each other.
Under the slab it is dry, the soil finer and warmer: seed storage, as Theron said.
A discovery: the east structure still does what it was built to do. +45 XP.

changes.note: Discovery: east structure seed storage kept dry by ghost-elm roots

event: She finds Hadley standing very still at the prayer-notch in the north wall.
A small pale plant grows in the dark cut: like a cave-pearl fern, a cave plant.
'The Rimfolk builder left that cut for the land's memory, and the land used it.'
Hadley realizes he spent three seasons gathering in someone's home without knowing.
'You pay attention, knowing someone else paid attention here first.' He starts to draw.
She rests her hand on the warm wall beside the notch and closes her eyes.
The notch holds intention layered through generations of tenants.
[Lay the Path] opens a second time in this place, more specific.
The bond seats as recognition: a place seen across generations, seen again.
BOND FORMED: Prayer-Notch, Glimpsed, trait [Tended], cluster node 2; +75 XP.

changes.note: Sympathetic Bond formed: Varethen prayer-notch, cluster node 2

event: Four bonds make six connections; the network grows like a ghost-elm grove.
Hadley is still drawing; she does not tell him.
He leaves at first light tomorrow for Millhaven, back in four days; she will write a letter.
At midday Maret steps out of the treeline from the east into the camp.
She is in her sixties, grey-white hair bound back, her face weathered in layers.
She looks at Wren like someone filing, takes Theron's tea, and sits at the south stone.
No one speaks; Theron stops Hadley with a look.
Wren drinks her tea and lets the fire speak.
After a long while: 'You hear them, don't you. The places.'
'They don't talk. They relay what they're feeling.' 'That's what she did.'
Maret tells of the Rootmother, who bonded places, and the places remembered her.
Her grandmother's grandmother felt it at the pool on a seventeenth night, the last time.
'And now you're here.' 'And now I'm here.'
Maret names the settlement: Varethen, the place that watches the road.
'The road is gone. But Varethen is still there?' 'It's there.' 'Good.'
After dinner Wren writes a short letter by firelight: four places, all well.
She sets it by Hadley's pack and writes in her journal: Day 5, 13 remain.
She wonders whether a place outlives its purpose, or its purpose sleeps in it.
Hadley leaves at first light with both letters, before the thrush calls.
The camp is quieter; Maret sits at the fire with Theron, taking only the space she needs.
Wren is at the east structure when Theron finds her.
'My father built here.' He was born in Varethen; they left when he was three.
His father never came back: nothing left to come back to. 'He was wrong.'
'He was wrong,' Theron agrees, and walks north toward camp.
She stays; the threshold stone was warm the whole time his father stayed away.
The sweetness is thinner here: the corruption cannot claim what is still occupied.
She thinks: I am occupying it. Not possessing; a tenancy the stone knows.
On the third day of Hadley's absence, Maret sits beside Wren at the camp's edge.
'Hadley will bring a name back from Millhaven.'
Someone young and restless has been asking about Wren at the supply post.
Brecca Vane, Aldric's niece, from Thorngate six months ago, has not found her class.
'She will come south. Names travel faster than feet.' Maret walks back to the fire.
Wren feels the ghost of a feeling from a girl she has never met, forty miles away.
Hadley returns on the fourth day, late afternoon, with two extra packs.
He hands Wren a letter from her mother.
By the fire she reads Sera's cramped hand while Hadley recounts Millhaven's news.
Her father has reread her first letter four times and studies his old basin notes.
Brecca has asked about her twice; she has the look of someone making a decision.
'Come home before first frost. That was the promise.'
She counts: Day 9, nine days left in the cycle. She writes it in the margin.
The falling numbers are a temporal map, like her father's river levels.
Maret asks if she is afraid. 'I don't know its shape yet.'
'Fear without a shape is useful. It keeps you paying attention.'
Wren writes that down as a field note and closes the journal.
She feels all four places through the network, six connections running in pairs.
She sleeps with four places and a name, the forest's tremor closer to weeping.
